title: What Happens to Spirit Airlines' Yellow Planes Now That It's Closed?
summary:
Have you ever seen a bright yellow Spirit Airlines plane and wondered where it goes when the airline stops flying? Spirit shut down last weekend, and now more than 90 of its planes are stuck at airports across the country. But here's the twist: Spirit doesn't even own most of them!

More than 60 planes are leased—like renting a car—and the real owners want them back fast. Steve Giordano runs a company that flies empty planes to storage. He says it's total chaos. "No one wants to touch them," he explains. His pilots, sometimes wearing jeans instead of uniforms, have to convince airport security to let them take the planes. "The first thing they're going to say is, 'no, no, no, no, no,'" Giordano says. Sometimes they even call the police!

Some planes will be leased to other airlines, some will have their engines removed, and others might be taken apart for spare parts. Spirit also owns 28 planes it can sell, plus an office building and repair shops. Even more valuable are its takeoff and landing slots at busy airports like LaGuardia in New York and Newark in New Jersey. Airlines will fight to buy those.

But there's a problem: jet fuel is super expensive right now—up about 70% since the war in Iran began. That makes Spirit's older, fuel-thirsty planes less attractive. Experts say selling everything might take longer than usual, but eventually, those yellow jets will find new homes.
why_it_matters: When a big airline closes, it can change ticket prices and airport jobs, and even bright yellow planes show how world events like wars far away can affect the things we use every day.

background_read: Spirit Airlines was a low-cost airline in the United States that charged cheap ticket prices but extra fees for luggage and snacks.
Airports like LaGuardia in New York are extremely busy, so landing slots—the right to land at a certain time—are rare and worth a lot of money.
Jet fuel prices have risen sharply since the war in Iran began, making older planes that burn more fuel harder to sell.
Article_Structure: WHO: Spirit Airlines (the closed airline), Steve Giordano (a plane mover), and other airlines that might buy the planes.
WHAT: Spirit shut down, leaving over 90 planes stranded; most were leased, so owners are rushing to get them back, leading to chaos and even police calls.
WHERE: Airports all across the United States, with valuable landing slots at LaGuardia in New York and Newark in New Jersey.
WHY: The airline ran out of money and stopped flying, and now its planes, building and airport slots must be sold to pay debts, though expensive fuel makes older planes tricky to sell.

perspectives.description: Other airlines might buy Spirit's planes and landing slots at a lower price, which could eventually lead to more flight choices or cheaper tickets for travellers.
Workers lose their jobs and passengers who had tickets may be stranded—this shows how sudden business failures can hurt many people.
Airlines often lease planes instead of buying them to save money, but when they close down it creates a messy scramble to return the aircraft to their real owners.
